catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-rebd:
Henry of Rebdorf is not a historical personage at all, but a name attached by error to a chronicle of empire and papacy spanning the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The only link to Rebdorf near Eichstätt is that its first editor published it from a manuscript preserved there, now in Paris, while other copies exist at Neuburg and Vienna. Its title, Chronica or Annales Imperatorum et Paparum, covers events from 1294 to 1362 in two parts.

The first part continues the Flores Temporum of a Swabian Franciscan to 1343 and was probably compiled about 1346 by an unknown writer. The second part, covering 1343 to 1363, was written by Heinrich Taub, called the Deaf, chaplain at St. Willibald's in Eichstätt, who died about 1364 and is known to have journeyed to Rome for the jubilee indulgence in 1350 and admired the crown jewels at Nuremberg in 1361. The chronicle's second part has real historical importance.

nasa-tm-19660006377-some-aspects-of-nois:
Gordon C Augason of the Space Sciences Division, with a colleague from the Instrumentation Division at Ames, analyzes noise in a kind of spectrometer that builds its spectrum in an unusual way. An interferometer spectrometer first records a pattern called an interferogram. A Fourier transform then turns that pattern into a spectrum. Noise in the pattern spreads through the result in ways that need care.

The authors use sampling theory and statistics to work out that spread. They then compare such instruments with conventional spectrometers on noise. Their check confirms a known gain, called Fellgett's advantage, for detectors not limited by background. The paper gives instrument builders a firmer basis for choosing between the two designs.
stifter-das-haidedorf:
A heath, a village, and the quiet lives between them fill Adalbert Stifter's early tale Das Haidedorf, given here in German. The Heath Village portrays rural Austrian life with his unmatched eye for landscape. Nothing loud happens, and that is precisely the point of Stifter's art.

He finds the extraordinary inside the ordinary: weather over the heath, work in the fields, a life unfolding at walking pace. Almost religious attention dignifies every scene he touches. Readers raised on faster fiction may need a page or two to slow down to his rhythm. The reward is a calm few modern writers can match. The tale makes a gentle introduction to a great and demanding author.
the-black-dwarf:
Sir Walter Scott's tale is presented inside a frame called Tales of My Landlord, collected by Jedediah Cleishbotham. That schoolmaster and parish clerk of Gandercleugh introduces himself at length. Contents separate his introduction, an introduction to the tale itself, and the main text.

Cleishbotham argues that Gandercleugh sits at the navel of Scotland, on routes between Edinburgh and Glasgow. Travellers rest at its Wallace Inn, where he has sat by the fire for forty years of evenings. From such talk, he implies, tales are gathered. Envy of merit, learning, and narrow local views are answered in a comic, self-important voice.
